terms: Feminism
Showalter Literature of Their Own 1977; Gilbert and Gubar Madwoman in Attic 1979; gynocriticism, female tradition.
Formalism and New Criticism
Brooks, Wimsatt 1930s-50s; intentional fallacy; close reading without biography; text as autonomous artefact.
Marxism
Lukacs, Eagleton; literature reflects class struggle; base-superstructure; ideology; Marxism and Literary Criticism 1976.
Psychoanalytic Criticism
Freud's Oedipus complex; Lacan's mirror stage and symbolic order; reads text as unconscious desire.
Reader-Response
Iser, Jauss 1970s; meaning produced in reading not text alone; horizon of expectations, implied reader.
Structuralism and Poststructuralism
Saussure's signifier/signified; Derrida's deconstruction 1967; meaning unstable; play of differences.

Williams Streetcar 1947
Tennessee Williams; Blanche DuBois faces brutal Stanley; Old South vs new America; desire and madness.
Dunkirk Evacuation
The 1940 retreat of British forces from France; McEwan's Part Two depicts Robbie's brutal march to the beaches.
St Thomas's Hospital
The London hospital where Briony trains as a nurse, encountering the bodily reality of war and her own complicity.
Sensory Prose
McEwan's wartime writing is dominated by smell, sound and touch — fragments of consciousness rather than panoramic narration.
Memory and Reconstruction
Briony's account is built from interviews, archives, and imagination; the novel foregrounds memory's textuality.
The Vase Scene
The 1935 fountain episode in which Cecilia undresses to retrieve the broken vase — observed and misread by Briony.
Liminality of the Body
Robbie's wounded body, Briony's nursing labour, and the violated body of Lola structure the novel's somatic ethics.
Country House Novel
A tradition McEwan inherits from Austen, Forster and Waugh; the Tallis estate functions as enclosed moral microcosm.
The Letter
Robbie's accidentally substituted note containing an obscene phrase ('cunt') — read by Briony, recoded as threat.
Class Asymmetry
Robbie is the housekeeper's son; the Tallises pay for his education but withdraw protection when accused.
Adolescent Imagination
Briony, aged thirteen, possesses literary ambition but lacks ethical experience; her misreading is shaped by genre.
Paul Marshall
The chocolate manufacturer who actually assaults Lola; his wartime profiteering and post-war marriage to Lola constitute the novel's unpunished crime.
Witness and Testimony
Briony's identification of Robbie at the temple is shaped not by sight but by pre-existing narrative — the novel anatomises legal witness as fiction.
Unreliable Narrator
A narrator whose account cannot be trusted; Briony's 1935 misreading and 1999 confession destabilise the entire text.
Metafiction
Fiction that draws attention to its own status as constructed; Atonement's coda reveals the preceding narrative as Briony's novel.
Three-Part Structure
1935 (the country house), 1940 (Dunkirk and the hospital), 1999 (Briony's confession) — a temporal architecture mirroring atonement's stages.
The Coda
The 'London, 1999' section in which Briony reveals she invented Robbie and Cecilia's reunion; their real fates were death and grief.
Intertextuality
McEwan draws on Austen (epigraph from Northanger Abbey), Woolf, Forster, and Rosamond Lehmann; Briony writes within an inherited tradition.
Atonement (Theme)
The novel asks whether art can ever make amends — and answers, with deliberate ambiguity, that it can only approximate.
Aristotelian Hamartia
Poetics: tragic hero's error or flaw causes downfall; Othello's jealousy, Macbeth's ambition, Lear's pride.
Bradley's Lectures 1904
Shakespearean Tragedy; character-based criticism; tragic hero exceptional but flawed; lasting influence.
Catharsis
Purgation of pity and fear in audience; tragedy's moral function; debated by AC Bradley (1904).
G. Wilson Knight Wheel of Fire 1930
Spatial pattern criticism; opposes Bradley's character focus; reads symbolic structures and imagery.
King Lear 1605
Aged king divides kingdom by daughters' flattery; Cordelia banished, Goneril and Regan turn; tragic recognition of madness.
Othello 1604
Moor of Venice manipulated by Iago into killing Desdemona; race, jealousy, manipulation; tragic Othello restores honour.
Blake Songs of Experience 1794
Innocence's dark counterpart; 'Tyger' and 'London'; critique of institutional oppression.
Keats Odes 1819
Wonder year: Nightingale, Grecian Urn, Autumn, Melancholy, Psyche; 'negative capability' theory.
Lyrical Ballads 1798
Wordsworth and Coleridge revolution; 'language really used by men'; preface to 1800 edition manifesto.
Shelley Defence of Poetry 1821
Poets as 'unacknowledged legislators of the world'; visionary politics; published posthumously 1840.
Sublime
Burke 1757 distinguished sublime (terror, vastness) from beautiful (delicacy); central to Romantic aesthetic.
Wordsworth Prelude
Autobiographical epic in blank verse; spots of time; growth of poet's mind; 1805 and 1850 versions.
Fallen Woman Trope
A Victorian narrative figure marked by lost sexual 'purity' and consequent social ruin; Hardy interrogates and subverts it.
Subtitle 'A Pure Woman'
Hardy's controversial 1891 subtitle that defends Tess's moral purity against Victorian convention, sparking outrage on publication.
Fate vs Free Will
The novel's central tension: characters appear driven by cosmic chance and heredity rather than autonomous choice.
Wessex
Hardy's semi-fictional reimagining of south-west England, a landscape that mirrors emotional and social states.
Paganism vs Christianity
Tess is linked to ancient sun-worship (Stonehenge climax) against the rigid, hypocritical Christianity of Angel and Alec.
Social Class and Heredity
The Durbeyfields' decayed aristocratic lineage drives the plot, exposing late-Victorian anxieties about class and inheritance.
Pathetic Fallacy
Projection of human emotion onto the natural environment; Hardy uses Talbothays' lushness and Flintcomb-Ash's barrenness to mirror Tess's states.
Talbothays Dairy
The pastoral idyll where Tess meets Angel; a fertile, milk-rich Eden contrasted with later landscapes of suffering.
Flintcomb-Ash
The bleak upland farm where Tess endures mechanised labour, symbolising industrial encroachment on rural life.
Mechanisation
The arrival of the steam threshing machine dramatises the displacement of traditional agricultural workers in the 1890s.
Phases of the Novel
Hardy structures Tess into seven 'Phases' (e.g. 'The Maiden', 'Maiden No More'), framing her life as ritualised stages.
Liminality
Hardy positions Tess on thresholds — between class, between innocence and experience — generating her tragic instability.
AO5 (Multiple Interpretations)
course Objective rewarding informed engagement with differing critical readings of the text.
Feminist Reading
Critics such as Penny Boumelha argue Tess is constructed as a sexualised object of the male gaze, even by Hardy's sympathetic narrator.
Marxist Reading
Critics like Raymond Williams read Tess's destruction as a product of capitalist enclosure and the disintegration of the rural working class.
Hamartia
Aristotelian 'tragic flaw'; for Tess, debated — is it her trust, her beauty, or simply her class position?
Narrative Voice
Hardy's narrator oscillates between sympathetic intimacy and detached, sometimes voyeuristic, observation.
Doubling
Tess's red ribbon, the slain horse Prince, the bloodstain on the ceiling — recurrent red motifs prefigure her death.

unit-4-internal-assessment-comparative-a.d: Unit 4: Internal course - Comparative and Contextual Study
terms: Biographical Criticism
Reads work through author's life; Plath's confessional poetry; criticised by New Criticism intentional fallacy.
Cultural Materialism
British Marxist; Dollimore and Sinfield Political Shakespeare 1985; contestation, dissident readings.
Eco-criticism
Lawrence Buell Environmental Imagination 1995; reads literature for ecological consciousness; nature writing tradition.
Historicism
Reads texts as products of historical conditions; e.g. Tillyard's Elizabethan World Picture 1943 for Shakespeare.
New Historicism
Greenblatt 1980s; texts and contexts mutually constitutive; Renaissance Self-Fashioning 1980.
Reception Theory
Jauss horizon of expectations; texts interpreted differently across periods; Hamlet's afterlife.
Historical Context
The social and political moment of a text's production — Restoration, Romantic, Modernist.
Social Context
Class, gender, race and economic conditions shaping characters and reception.
Critical Reception
How a text was read at the time and since — Leavis on Lawrence, Said on Conrad.
Intertextuality
Kristeva's term — every text is a tissue of citations from prior texts.
Adaptation and Reception History
How later versions (film, stage, novelisation) shape current readings.
Diachronic Comparison
Comparing texts from different periods to trace continuity and change.
Form Comparison
Comparing genre and macro-shape (sonnet vs dramatic monologue, novel vs novella).
Structural Comparison
Comparing the arrangement of parts (linear vs disrupted, framed vs continuous).
Figurative Comparison
Comparing imagery, metaphor and symbol systems across texts.
Stylistic Register
Comparing diction, syntax and tone — Latinate vs Anglo-Saxon, formal vs colloquial.
Voice Comparison
Comparing narrators or speakers — reliability, distance, focalisation.
Effect on Reader
Comparing how each text positions its reader — sympathetic, ironic, distanced.
Comparative Reading
Setting two or more texts side by side to highlight similarities and differences in theme, technique and context.
Thematic Axis
A shared topic (power, gender, mortality) along which two texts can be aligned for comparison.
Connective Vocabulary
Phrases like 'similarly', 'whereas', 'by contrast' that signal comparative moves to the reader.
Symmetrical vs Asymmetrical Comparison
Symmetrical treats both texts equally; asymmetrical uses one text to illuminate the other.
Tertium Comparationis
The third term — the framework against which two texts are compared.
Convergence and Divergence
Where texts agree, and where they diverge — both are fertile for argument.
Feminist Criticism
Reading literature for its construction and critique of gender (Woolf, Showalter, Gilbert & Gubar, Cixous).
Gynocriticism
Elaine Showalter's term — feminist criticism focused on women writers and their traditions.
Madwoman in the Attic
Gilbert and Gubar (1979) — patriarchal literature's confinement of women between angel and monster.
Freudian Criticism
Reading for unconscious desires, repression, the Oedipus complex and dream-work.
Lacanian Criticism
Reading through Jacques Lacan's mirror stage, the symbolic order and the Real.
Écriture Féminine
Hélène Cixous's term — feminine writing that disrupts patriarchal language (The Laugh of the Medusa, 1975).
Post-Structuralism
Movement (Derrida, Barthes, Foucault) destabilising structuralist certainties about meaning, sign and subject.
Death of the Author
Roland Barthes (1967) — the author does not control meaning; the reader produces it.
Deconstruction
Jacques Derrida's strategy for reading the contradictions and supplements within seemingly stable binaries.
Reader-Response Criticism
Approach (Iser, Fish) treating meaning as produced in the reader's encounter with the text.
Iser's Implied Reader
Wolfgang Iser's idea that texts contain gaps the reader fills, constituting an implied reader role.
Interpretive Communities
Stanley Fish's term — meaning is determined by communities of readers sharing interpretive strategies.
Formalism
Critical approach (Russian Formalists, New Criticism) focused on the autonomous text — form, image, ambiguity.
Defamiliarisation
Shklovsky's term — art renews perception by making the familiar strange (ostranenie).
New Criticism
Anglo-American formalism (Brooks, Wimsatt) advocating close reading and the intentional fallacy.
Marxist Criticism
Approach reading literature as shaped by class, ideology and economic base (Eagleton, Williams).
Base and Superstructure
Marx's model — economic base shapes the cultural superstructure (art, law, religion).
Ideology
Althusser — the imaginary relation of subjects to their real conditions of existence, reproduced in texts.
Aristotelian Hamartia
Poetics: tragic hero's error or flaw causes downfall; Othello's jealousy, Macbeth's ambition, Lear's pride.
Bradley's Lectures 1904
Shakespearean Tragedy; character-based criticism; tragic hero exceptional but flawed; lasting influence.
Catharsis

G. Wilson Knight Wheel of Fire 1930

Othello 1604

Bildungsroman
Coming-of-age narrative tracing moral and psychological growth; Goethe's Wilhelm Meister 1796 set the template; Joyce's Portrait of the Artist a modern instance.
Epistolary novel
Narrative told through letters or documents; Samuel Richardson's Pamela 1740 and Mary Shelley's Frankenstein 1818 use this form.
Free indirect discourse
Third-person narration coloured by a character's voice without quotation marks; pioneered by Jane Austen in Emma 1815.
Magic realism
Fusion of realistic settings with matter-of-fact magical elements; Gabriel Garcia Marquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude 1967 is the canonical example.
Novel of manners
Genre satirising social customs of a defined class; Austen's Pride and Prejudice 1813 and Edith Wharton's Age of Innocence 1920 are paradigms.
Unreliable narrator
Wayne Booth's 1961 term for narrators whose account the reader must distrust; Nabokov's Humbert Humbert in Lolita 1955 typifies it.

Shelley Defence of Poetry 1821
Poets as 'unacknowledged legislators of the world'; visionary politics; published posthumously 1840.
Sublime
Burke 1757 distinguished sublime (terror, vastness) from beautiful (delicacy); central to Romantic aesthetic.
Wordsworth Prelude
Autobiographical epic in blank verse; spots of time; growth of poet's mind; 1805 and 1850 versions.
The Vampire Bite
Penetrative, mouth-to-throat, fluid-exchanging; Christopher Craft reads it as coded queer/heterosexual transgression.
Lucy's Transformation
Lucy moves from chaste fiancée to predatory 'bloofer lady'; her staking is staged with explicit sexual violence.
Mina's Resistance
Mina, partially vamped, retains agency, drives the documentary archive, and locates Dracula via hypnotic link.
The Three Sisters
The female vampires at Castle Dracula who attempt to seduce Harker; embody overt female sexual aggression.
Christopher Craft's Reading
Craft's 'Kiss Me with Those Red Lips' (1984) reads the vampire's mouth as a site of unstable gender and queer desire.
Blood Transfusion
Lucy receives blood from Arthur, Seward, Van Helsing, and Quincey — a quasi-sexual circulation Arthur calls a 'marriage'.
Castle Dracula
The Borgo Pass castle, dilapidated and labyrinthine; Gothic prototype of confinement and aristocratic decay.
The Demeter
The schooner that carries Dracula from Varna to Whitby; the captain's log is one of the novel's most powerful set-pieces.
Whitby
The Yorkshire seaside town where Dracula makes landfall; Stoker visited in 1890 and based Dracula's arrival on local folklore.
Carfax
The decayed London estate Dracula purchases as his base; a Gothic ruin embedded in the modern metropolis.
Technology
Typewriters, phonographs, shorthand, telegrams, Kodak cameras, blood transfusion — modernity's tools weaponised against the ancient.
The Crew of Light
Christopher Craft's name for the male hunters (Harker, Seward, Holmwood, Morris, Van Helsing) who pursue Dracula.
Epistolary Form
A novel composed of letters, diary entries, news cuttings, and phonograph transcripts; Stoker's form mimics evidentiary accumulation.
Fin de Siècle
The 'end of the century' (1890s) atmosphere of decadence, decline, and anxiety over degeneration.
Reverse Colonisation
Stephen Arata's term (1990) for the anxiety that the colonial periphery (Transylvania) might invade and contaminate the imperial centre (London).
New Woman
1890s figure of female emancipation; Mina exhibits 'New Woman' competence (stenography, intellect) while remaining domestically anchored.
Lucy and Mina
Stoker's dual heroines: Lucy is sexualised, infected and destroyed; Mina is intellectual, infected and saved — a Madonna/whore split.
Van Helsing's Polyglossia
Van Helsing's mangled English, scientific authority, and folkloric knowledge model Stoker's hybrid epistemology — modern + ancient.
Vitalism Debate
Early-19th-century controversy between John Abernethy (vital principle) and William Lawrence (materialism); Percy Shelley was Lawrence's patient.
Natural Philosophy
The pre-modern term for science; Victor studies Agrippa, Paracelsus, Albertus Magnus (occult), then Krempe and Waldman (modern).
Sublime Landscape
Mont Blanc, Chamonix, the Mer de Glace — the Alpine sublime mirrors Victor's transgressive ambition and the Creature's solitude.
Domesticity
The Frankenstein household and the De Lacey cottage embody the bourgeois ideal Victor's ambition destroys.
Nature vs Nurture
The Creature insists he is born benevolent and made evil by exclusion; the novel stages an early-Romantic environmentalist argument.
Enlightenment Critique
The novel interrogates the Enlightenment faith in reason and progress, exposing its ethical blind spots.
Doppelganger
Gothic figure of the double or shadow self; Victor and the Creature are read as halves of a single divided psyche.
The Uncanny
Freud's unheimlich (1919); the familiar made disturbing. The Creature embodies the uncanny via familiar parts assembled monstrously.
Paradise Lost
Milton's 1667 epic; the Creature reads it and identifies first with Adam, then with Satan. The novel's epigraph is from PL X.743–5.
Education of the Creature
The De Lacey episode: the Creature observes a French family, learning language, history (Volney's Ruins), and the structure of social rejection.
Sympathy
An Enlightenment ethical category (Adam Smith); the Creature seeks it, is denied it, and the novel asks the reader to extend it.
The Female Creature
Victor destroys the half-finished female companion in the Orkneys; this refusal triggers the Creature's revenge on Elizabeth.
Romanticism
Late-18th/early-19th-century movement valuing imagination, nature, and individual subjectivity; Shelley engages and critiques it.
Promethean Myth
Greek myth of the Titan who steals fire from the gods; Shelley's subtitle 'The Modern Prometheus' frames Victor as transgressor.
Gothic Conventions
Atmospheric setting, doubling, transgression, the uncanny, supernatural intrusion — Shelley fuses Gothic with Enlightenment science.
Frame Narrative
Walton's letters frame Victor's narrative, which frames the Creature's; nested narration foregrounds testimony and reliability.
Sublime
Burkean and Kantian category of overwhelming, terrifying grandeur; the Alps and Arctic embody it, mirroring Victor's ambition.
Galvanism
Luigi Galvani's late-18th-century experiments with electricity and frog legs; haunts Shelley's vivification scene without being named.
Revenge Tragedy
Genre popularised by Kyd's The Spanish Tragedy (1587); features ghost, delay, madness real or feigned, play-within-a-play, bloody finale.
Soliloquy
A speech delivered alone on stage, granting audience access to a character's interiority; Hamlet has seven major soliloquies.
Hamartia
Aristotelian 'tragic flaw'; for Hamlet, variously identified as melancholy, indecision, intellectualism, or moral scruple.
The Ghost
Old Hamlet's spectre, theologically ambiguous (purgatorial Catholic? demonic Protestant?) — a hermeneutic crisis as much as a plot device.
Antic Disposition
Hamlet's feigned madness, declared at 1.5; its boundaries with real disturbance remain critically contested.
Quarto and Folio Texts
Q1 (1603, 'bad quarto'), Q2 (1604/5, longest), F1 (1623); textual variants make 'Hamlet' a plural work.
Oedipal Reading
Freud (1900) and Ernest Jones (1949) argue Hamlet's delay reflects unconscious identification with Claudius, who has acted out Hamlet's repressed desires.
Bradleian Character Criticism
A.C. Bradley's Shakespearean Tragedy (1904) treats Hamlet as a coherent psychological subject with a 'melancholy' temperament.
New Historicism
Stephen Greenblatt's Hamlet in Purgatory (2001) reads the play through Reformation theology and the suppression of Catholic purgatory.
Feminist Criticism
Elaine Showalter's 'Representing Ophelia' (1985) recovers Ophelia from male critical projection, attending to her madness as social statement.
Performance Criticism
Readings rooted in stage history — Olivier (1948), Branagh (1996), Almereyda (2000) — show how each generation reinvents the play.
Memorial Reconstruction
Theory that Q1 was reconstructed by an actor from memory; critics like Paul Werstine challenge this, complicating textual hierarchy.
Metatheatre
Theatre that draws attention to its own theatricality; Hamlet's players, advice to actors, and play-within-play are constitutive.
The Mousetrap
Hamlet's adapted play The Murder of Gonzago, staged in 3.2 to 'catch the conscience of the king'.
Player King's Speech
The Aeneas-to-Dido speech the First Player delivers about Pyrrhus and Hecuba; prompts Hamlet's 'rogue and peasant slave' soliloquy.
Doubling
Hamlet/Laertes, Hamlet/Fortinbras, Old Hamlet/Claudius — character pairings that test Hamlet's identity against alternatives.
Yorick
The dead jester whose skull Hamlet contemplates in 5.1; embodiment of memento mori and the limits of theatrical illusion.
Advice to the Players
Hamlet's 3.2 instructions to the players articulate a poetics of restrained, naturalistic acting — read as Shakespeare's own.
Deconstruction
Derrida's reading practice exposing how texts undermine their own oppositional certainties.
Différance
Derrida's portmanteau (1968) of difference and deferral — meaning never arrives whole.
Logocentrism
Western philosophy's privileging of speech, presence and centred meaning, which deconstruction critiques.
Trace
Derrida — the mark of what is absent within what is present; every sign carries the trace of others.
Supplement
The 'extra' element that turns out to be constitutive of what it merely supposed to supplement (writing to speech, in Plato).
Yale School
American deconstructionists (de Man, Hartman, Hillis Miller) extending Derrida's work to literature.
Orientalism
Edward Said (1978) — Western knowledge of 'the East' produces and supports imperial power.
The Other
Post-colonial critics analyse how Western texts construct non-European peoples as different and inferior.
Subaltern
Gayatri Spivak — those outside hegemonic discourse; her essay 'Can the Subaltern Speak?' (1988) questions their representation.
Hybridity
Homi Bhabha — the in-between space where colonial cultures mix and resist.
Mimicry
Bhabha — colonised subjects imitate the coloniser, producing a partial, destabilising likeness.
Writing Back
Post-colonial writers (Achebe, Rhys, Walcott) rewrite canonical texts from the margins.
New Criticism
Anglo-American formalist school (Brooks, Ransom, Wimsatt) advocating close reading of the autonomous text.
Intentional Fallacy
Wimsatt & Beardsley (1946) — appealing to authorial intention is fallacious; the text is sovereign.
Affective Fallacy
Wimsatt & Beardsley — appealing to reader emotion is also fallacious.
Structuralism
Movement (Saussure, Lévi-Strauss, Barthes early) treating culture as a system of signs.
Signifier and Signified
Saussure's two halves of the sign — the sound-image and the concept; relation is arbitrary.
Binary Opposition
Lévi-Strauss — culture organises meaning through binary pairs (raw/cooked, nature/culture).
Eliot Waste Land 1922
Fragmented epic of post-WWI Europe; allusions to Dante, Buddhist sermons; 'shored against my ruins'.
HD (Hilda Doolittle)
Imagist; classical refigured ('Helen', 'Sea Garden'); sharp imagery, free verse.
Pound Make It New
Imagism 1934 (the book title); In a Station of the Metro; 'direct treatment of the thing'; clarity, concision.
Stein Tender Buttons 1914
Gertrude Stein's Cubist prose poetry; cuts ordinary language to renew perception.
Williams Red Wheelbarrow
1923; 'so much depends'; American Imagism; everyday objects with attention; against Eliot's tradition.
Yeats Tower Period
Second Coming 1919-20; 'things fall apart; the centre cannot hold'; mysticism and Irish history.
Genette's Narrative Discourse (1972)
Foundational narratological study analysing Proust through systematic categories.
Focalisation
Whose perspective filters narrative information — zero, internal or external.
Narrative Voice
Who speaks — heterodiegetic (outside) or homodiegetic (inside) the story.
Narrative Order
The relation between story-time and discourse-time — analepsis (flashback), prolepsis (flash-forward).
Narrative Duration
How story-time maps to discourse-time — scene, summary, ellipsis, pause.
Frequency
How often events are told relative to occurrence — singulative, repetitive, iterative.
Fabula
Russian Formalist term — the chronological events as they 'really' happened in the story-world.
Sjuzhet
The arrangement and presentation of those events as the reader encounters them (also called plot).
Story / Discourse
Genette's parallel pair (histoire / récit) — events told versus telling.
Implied Author
Wayne Booth's term — the textual personality the reader infers, distinct from the historical author.
Implied Reader
Wolfgang Iser — the reader role inscribed in the text, the receiver the text seems to imagine.
Narrative Levels
Genette distinguishes extradiegetic (outside the story), diegetic (within), metadiegetic (a story-within-a-story).
Propp's Morphology
Vladimir Propp (1928) analysed 100 Russian folktales and identified 31 recurring narrative functions in a fixed order.
Functions
Propp's units of action — absentation, prohibition, violation, villainy, struggle, victory, return etc.
Character Roles
Propp identified seven character spheres: hero, villain, helper, donor, princess, dispatcher, false hero.
Structuralist Inheritance
Propp influenced Lévi-Strauss, Barthes and modern screenwriting templates.
Hero's Journey
Joseph Campbell (1949) extracted a mythic monomyth pattern overlapping with Propp's functions.
Greimas's Actants
A. J. Greimas refined Propp into six actantial roles arranged in three oppositional pairs.

non-exam-assessment-literature-post-1900.d: Non-exam course: Literature post-1900 (Close Reading and Comparative Essay)
terms: Angry Young Men
1950s movement: Osborne's Look Back in Anger 1956, Amis Lucky Jim 1954; class resentment, anti-establishment.
Black British Poetry
Linton Kwesi Johnson, Grace Nichols; Patience Agbabi; reframes English tradition with Caribbean and African voices.
Carter Bloody Chamber 1979
Angela Carter's feminist fairy tale rewrites; subverts Bluebeard, Beauty and Beast; magical realism.
Heaney North 1975
Bog poems use Iron Age bodies to address Northern Ireland Troubles; Catholic Irish poet; Nobel 1995.
Larkin The Less Deceived 1955
The Movement; plain diction, anti-modernist; ironic Englishness; 'Church Going', 'Whitsun Weddings'.
Plath Ariel 1965
Confessional poetry; 'Daddy', 'Lady Lazarus'; published posthumously after 1963 suicide; Bell Jar same year.

paper-1-drama-and-poetry-pre-1900-includ.d: Paper 1: Drama and Poetry pre-1900 (including Shakespeare)
terms: Aristotelian Hamartia
Poetics: tragic hero's error or flaw causes downfall; Othello's jealousy, Macbeth's ambition, Lear's pride.
Bradley's Lectures 1904
Shakespearean Tragedy; character-based criticism; tragic hero exceptional but flawed; lasting influence.
Catharsis
Purgation of pity and fear in audience; tragedy's moral function; debated by AC Bradley (1904).
G. Wilson Knight Wheel of Fire 1930
Spatial pattern criticism; opposes Bradley's character focus; reads symbolic structures and imagery.
King Lear 1605
Aged king divides kingdom by daughters' flattery; Cordelia banished, Goneril and Regan turn; tragic recognition of madness.
Othello 1604
Moor of Venice manipulated by Iago into killing Desdemona; race, jealousy, manipulation; tragic Othello restores honour.
Biographical Criticism
Reads work through author's life; Plath's confessional poetry; criticised by New Criticism intentional fallacy.
Cultural Materialism
British Marxist; Dollimore and Sinfield Political Shakespeare 1985; contestation, dissident readings.
Eco-criticism
Lawrence Buell Environmental Imagination 1995; reads literature for ecological consciousness; nature writing tradition.
Historicism
Reads texts as products of historical conditions; e.g. Tillyard's Elizabethan World Picture 1943 for Shakespeare.
New Historicism
Greenblatt 1980s; texts and contexts mutually constitutive; Renaissance Self-Fashioning 1980.
Reception Theory
Jauss horizon of expectations; texts interpreted differently across periods; Hamlet's afterlife.
Comparative analysis
Reading two or more poems alongside each other to explore similarities and differences in meaning, method and effect, rather than treating each in isolation.
Connective language
Linking words and phrases such as 'similarly', 'whereas' and 'in contrast' that signal comparison and keep two texts in dialogue within a response.
Context (AO3)
The historical, social and biographical circumstances of each poem, which can help explain why paired poems treat a shared subject differently.
Convergence and divergence
The ways poems agree (converge) or differ (diverge) in attitude, tone or method, which a comparative response should weigh and explain.
Integrated comparison
An essay structure that discusses both poems together point by point, rather than analysing one poem fully before turning to the other.
Point of comparison
A shared theme, image, form or technique that gives a clear basis for comparison, such as two poems both treating grief or both using the sonnet form.
Morality Play
Medieval allegorical drama (e.g. Everyman, c.1500) in which abstract virtues and vices contend for the soul; Marlowe's Good and Bad Angels are direct inheritances.
Renaissance Humanism
Recovery of classical learning, emphasis on human capacity and intellectual ambition; Faustus exemplifies its dangerous extremity.
Necromancy
The conjuring of spirits; Faustus's chosen art, theologically distinct from natural magic and condemned by both Protestant and Catholic authorities.
Mephistopheles
Faustus's attendant devil; theologically lucid, often warns Faustus, and embodies the tragedy of self-aware damnation.
Calvinist Theology
Doctrine of predestination — the elect and reprobate are eternally determined; complicates whether Faustus could ever have been saved.
The Seven Deadly Sins Pageant
In 2.3 Lucifer parades Pride, Covetousness, Wrath, Envy, Gluttony, Sloth, Lechery before Faustus — a direct morality-play borrowing.
A-Text (1604)
Quarto published 1604; shorter (around 1,500 lines), often considered closer to Marlowe's autograph by editors like Bevington & Rasmussen.
B-Text (1616)
Quarto published 1616; longer (around 2,100 lines), includes added comic scenes likely written by Samuel Rowley and William Birde in 1602.
Henslowe's Diary
Philip Henslowe records a 1602 payment of £4 to Birde and Rowley for additions to Faustus; documentary basis for B-text additions.
The Bevington Edition
David Bevington and Eric Rasmussen's Revels parallel-text edition (1993) sets A and B side by side and remains the scholarly standard.
Comic Subplot
Robin and Rafe (A) / Robin and Dick (B) parody Faustus's magic; the B-text expands these scenes, generating critical debate about tonal coherence.
Devotional Closure
Both texts end with the Chorus's 'Cut is the branch'; but the B-text adds a final scene with the scholars discovering Faustus's mangled limbs.
The Twenty-Four Years
Faustus's contract grants him twenty-four years of service from Mephistopheles in exchange for his soul.
Trivial Magic
What Faustus actually does — gulling the Pope, fetching grapes for the Duchess of Vanholt — is bathetically banal; critics read this as deliberate.
Helen of Troy
Faustus conjures Helen in 5.1; his apostrophe ('Was this the face that launched a thousand ships?') is both lyric apex and theological catastrophe.
The Old Man
Late morality figure who counsels repentance in 5.1; his persistence under devilish assault contrasts with Faustus's despair.
Final Monologue
The 5.2 hour-long soliloquy in which Faustus measures damnation against fleeing time; one of the most prosodically dense speeches in Renaissance drama.
Mighty Line
Ben Jonson's term for Marlowe's blank verse — propulsive, hyperbolic, declamatory; Faustus showcases it throughout.
Cinthio's Hecatommithi
Giraldi Cinthio's 1565 Italian novella collection; the seventh story of the third decade provides Shakespeare's plot — 'Disdemona' and an unnamed 'Moor'.
Tragic Hero
Aristotelian protagonist of stature whose hamartia precipitates downfall; Othello's stature is racially marked, his fall amplified.
Jealousy as Theme
Iago calls it 'the green-eyed monster'; the play anatomises jealousy as epistemic rather than purely emotional — a way of misreading the world.
Iago
The play's longest part (more lines than Othello); a Vice-figure descendant who weaponises his audience access through soliloquy.
Race and Moorishness
Othello is repeatedly called 'Moor', 'thick-lips', 'the Barbary horse' — Shakespeare stages early modern racial categories with critical sharpness.
Domestic Tragedy
The play borrows from the emerging genre of bourgeois domestic tragedy (Arden of Faversham, A Woman Killed with Kindness) by locating tragedy in marriage.
Soliloquy and Address
Iago has more soliloquies than any other character (eight), positioning the audience as confidants — a structural ethical bind.
Motiveless Malignity
Coleridge's 1818 phrase for Iago's motivation; suggests he offers reasons (promotion, rumour of cuckoldry, lust for Desdemona) without committing to any.
The Vice
Medieval morality figure who delighted audiences through duplicity; Iago is the Vice's Renaissance descendant, sharing the audience's view of the action.
Honest Iago
The word 'honest' is applied to Iago over fifty times in the play; Shakespeare weaponises the Renaissance ideal of plain-speaking masculinity.
Cassio's Reputation
Iago's manipulation of Cassio through drink and brawling exposes the male homosocial economy of reputation that he later exploits with Othello.
The Handkerchief
Desdemona's strawberry-spotted handkerchief — a maternal heirloom rendered evidentiary; T.S. Rymer mocked it, but it indexes the play's economy of proof.
Desdemona's Agency
She elopes against her father's wishes, defends Othello in the Senate (1.3), and answers Othello's accusations with intelligence; her later passivity is contested critically.
Emilia's Realism
Iago's wife and Desdemona's confidante; her 4.3 'willow scene' speech is a remarkable defence of female equality and adultery's mutual cause.
Bianca
Cassio's lover, often dismissed as a 'courtesan'; her jealousy over the handkerchief in 4.1 ironically mirrors Othello's.
Willow Song
The folk lament Desdemona sings in 4.3, inherited from her mother's maid Barbary; its grief prefigures her own death.
Smothering
Othello kills Desdemona in 5.2 by smothering (not stabbing); the bedroom murder transforms domestic intimacy into tragic stage.
Feminist Criticism
Critics including Carol Thomas Neely, Lisa Jardine, and Dympna Callaghan reread the women as substantive characters resisting patriarchal closure.
Frame Narrative
Lockwood, the southern outsider tenant of Thrushcross Grange, frames Nelly Dean's interior narration of the Earnshaw-Linton history.
Lockwood
Naive, snobbish, and unreliable; his misreadings (of Catherine's diary, of Heathcliff's character) prime the reader to be sceptical.
Nelly Dean
Housekeeper and lifelong witness; her narration is intimate but partisan — she dislikes Heathcliff and favours the Lintons.
Lockwood arrives in 1801, returns in 1802; the action stretches back to 1771 (Heathcliff's arrival as a child).
Diary and Document
Catherine's marginalia in Lockwood's borrowed books opens the past; the novel embeds textual layers within the oral frame.
Publication
Published in three volumes in December 1847 under 'Ellis Bell'; Charlotte's 1850 preface introduced Emily's name and softened reception.
Byronic Hero
Romantic protagonist after Byron's Childe Harold and Manfred: brooding, transgressive, mysterious origin, alienated from social norms.
Heathcliff's Origin
Brought from Liverpool by old Mr Earnshaw; his racial identity is ambiguous (called 'dark', 'gipsy', 'Lascar'); critics debate the novel's relation to the Atlantic slave trade.
Doubled Identity
Catherine's 'I am Heathcliff' (Ch. 9) declares fused identity; the novel literalises Gothic doubling beyond metaphor.
Revenge Plot
After Catherine's marriage to Edgar, Heathcliff returns mysteriously wealthy and methodically destroys both families through marriage and inheritance.
Gothic Inheritance
Brontë's Gothic fuses Radcliffean atmosphere with German Romanticism (Hoffmann); the supernatural is sustained but never settled.
Postcolonial Readings
Critics including Susan Meyer and Elsie Michie read Heathcliff's racial coding as central; the novel registers Britain's imperial guilt obliquely.
The Moors
The bleak Yorkshire upland between the Heights and the Grange; a Romantic-Gothic landscape that mirrors and resists human passion.
Two Houses
Wuthering Heights (high, windswept, primitive) and Thrushcross Grange (low, enclosed, civilised); Brontë's spatial dialectic.
The Second Generation
Young Cathy Linton, Linton Heathcliff, Hareton Earnshaw; their narrative occupies the second half of the novel.
Hareton's Recovery
Educated by Cathy after Heathcliff's death; his learning to read symbolises the second generation's tentative repair.
Reading and Literacy
Catherine's marginalia, Hareton's illiteracy, Linton's letters — books and writing structure power across the novel.
Ambiguous Closure
The final image — sleepers in 'that quiet earth' — is undercut by the shepherd boy's report of ghosts walking; resolution is denied.
Blake Songs of Experience 1794
Innocence's dark counterpart; 'Tyger' and 'London'; critique of institutional oppression.
Keats Odes 1819
Wonder year: Nightingale, Grecian Urn, Autumn, Melancholy, Psyche; 'negative capability' theory.
Lyrical Ballads 1798
Wordsworth and Coleridge revolution; 'language really used by men'; preface to 1800 edition manifesto.
Shelley Defence of Poetry 1821
Poets as 'unacknowledged legislators of the world'; visionary politics; published posthumously 1840.
Sublime
Burke 1757 distinguished sublime (terror, vastness) from beautiful (delicacy); central to Romantic aesthetic.
Wordsworth Prelude
Autobiographical epic in blank verse; spots of time; growth of poet's mind; 1805 and 1850 versions.
Orientalism (1978)
Edward Said's foundational study — Western academic and aesthetic representations of 'the East' produced and supported colonial power.
Foucauldian Frame
Said borrows Foucault's idea that knowledge and power are inseparable — discourse produces what it claims to describe.
Imaginative Geography
Said's term for the symbolic mapping of self and other onto territory.
Latent and Manifest Orientalism
Said distinguishes the persistent unconscious orientalist substrate from its surface manifestations.
Othering
The discursive construction of a group as different and inferior — a key post-colonial mechanism.
Culture and Imperialism (1993)
Said's sequel reading canonical novels (Mansfield Park, Heart of Darkness) for their imperial assumptions.
Hybridity
Homi Bhabha (The Location of Culture, 1994) — the productive in-between of colonial cultures.
Mimicry
Bhabha — the colonised's partial imitation of the coloniser, producing 'almost the same but not quite'.
Third Space
Bhabha's term for the in-between zone where identities are negotiated and remade.
Achebe on Conrad
Chinua Achebe's 1975 lecture branded Heart of Darkness racist, reframing canonical reception.
Writing Back
Post-colonial novelists rewrite canonical texts (Rhys's Wide Sargasso Sea reworks Jane Eyre).
Counter-discourse
Texts that contest the assumptions of dominant discourse — Achebe's Things Fall Apart against colonial fictions of Africa.
Subaltern
Gayatri Spivak — those outside hegemonic discourse, whose speech is mediated, translated and often distorted.
Can the Subaltern Speak? (1988)
Spivak's foundational essay examining the impossibility of hearing the subaltern within colonial archives.
Strategic Essentialism
Spivak's term for the political use of essentialist categories despite their theoretical problems.
Worlding
Heidegger via Spivak — how a Western text imaginatively constitutes the colonised world.
Epistemic Violence
The violence of imposing Western categories on non-Western knowledges, erasing local frameworks.
Translation Problems
Spivak argues every translation across cultural boundaries risks losing voice.
Free Indirect Discourse (FID)
Third-person narration that adopts a character's idiom and viewpoint without quotation marks ('She wondered. Was it really Tuesday again?').
Focalisation
Genette's term — the perspective through which events are presented; internal, external or zero.
Direct Discourse
Reported speech with quotation marks: 'She said, "I am tired."'
Indirect Discourse
Reported speech without quotation marks: 'She said she was tired.'
Narrative Distance
The perceived closeness between narrator and character, modulated by FID and focalisation.
Style Indirect Libre
French term for FID, especially associated with Flaubert's Madame Bovary.
Setting
The temporal and spatial world of the text; not background but active meaning-maker.
Symbol
A concrete image (Gatsby's green light, the conch in Lord of the Flies) that gathers larger meaning.
Structure
The arrangement of parts — chapters, sections, framing devices, chronological vs disrupted order.
In Medias Res
Beginning in the middle of action, common in modernist and contemporary fiction.
Frame Narrative
A story within a story (Frankenstein's three nested narrators, Heart of Darkness).
Narrative Time
Manipulation of duration, frequency and order (Genette) — flashback, summary, scene.
First-Person Narration
The narrator is a character within the story (I went.), offering immediacy and bias.
Third-Person Omniscient
Narrator stands outside the story with access to all characters' thoughts and events.
Third-Person Limited
Narrator stands outside but restricts knowledge to one character's perspective.
Unreliable Narrator
Wayne Booth (1961) — narrator whose account the reader is invited to distrust.
Second-Person Narration
Rare 'you' narration (Bright Lights, Big City) that implicates the reader.
Multiple Narrators
Texts using several first-person voices (The Sound and the Fury, As I Lay Dying).
Aristotelian Hamartia
Poetics: tragic hero's error or flaw causes downfall; Othello's jealousy, Macbeth's ambition, Lear's pride.
Bradley's Lectures 1904
Shakespearean Tragedy; character-based criticism; tragic hero exceptional but flawed; lasting influence.
Catharsis
Purgation of pity and fear in audience; tragedy's moral function; debated by AC Bradley (1904).
G. Wilson Knight Wheel of Fire 1930
Spatial pattern criticism; opposes Bradley's character focus; reads symbolic structures and imagery.
King Lear 1605
Aged king divides kingdom by daughters' flattery; Cordelia banished, Goneril and Regan turn; tragic recognition of madness.
Othello 1604
Moor of Venice manipulated by Iago into killing Desdemona; race, jealousy, manipulation; tragic Othello restores honour.
Enjambment and caesura
Enjambment runs a sentence over a line break without pause, while a caesura is a pause within a line; both control a poem's pace and emphasis.
Form and structure
The overall shape of a poem, including stanza length, line breaks, rhyme scheme and turning points, which guide how its meaning unfolds.
Imagery
Language that appeals to the senses or creates mental pictures, including metaphor, simile and personification, which shapes a poem's mood and meaning.
Metre and rhythm
The pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in a poem; a regular metre such as iambic pentameter creates a beat that poets may disrupt for effect.
Tone and voice
The attitude and mood conveyed by the speaker, and the identity of the speaking persona, which may differ from the poet themselves.
Unseen poetry analysis
The skill of closely reading a poem you have not studied before, working out its meaning, methods and effects within the time limit of an exam.
